ingenious: clever and inventive; showing skill in devising or making things
printing-house: a workshop where books and newspapers were printed
manuscript: an author's handwritten or typed draft before it is printed
tallow-chandler: a maker of candles from animal fat, the trade of Franklin's father
short-hand: a fast system of abbreviated symbols used for writing speech quickly
quarto: a book size made by folding each sheet into four leaves
joint-stool: a simple wooden stool made with mortised joints, not upholstered
indentures: formal written contracts binding an apprentice to a master
apprentice: a young person bound by contract to learn a trade from a master
conventicles: secret or unlawful religious meetings, especially of dissenters
sterling: British money of standard value, used as a mark of genuine worth
scrivener: a person who copied out documents and drew up legal papers
errata: a list of printing mistakes found after a book was printed
bisket: a hard, dry biscuit kept for long sea voyages
wharf: a landing place built on the water where ships load and unload
composing: setting type by hand for printing a page
press: the printing press used to make copies of a page
lightning: the electric flash of a storm, studied by Franklin in his experiments
electricity: the natural force of electric charge, which Franklin investigated
satire: writing that mocks people or society to expose their faults
diplomacy: the conduct of negotiations and relations between nations
homely: plain, simple, and practical rather than elegant or refined
vulgar: common or coarse, lacking refinement or good taste
sober: serious, plain, and moderate, without show or excess
pious: devoutly religious, showing reverence for God
genteel: polite and refined, belonging to good society
diffidence: a lack of self-confidence, shyness about one's own abilities
artful: crafty and skilled at arranging things to one's advantage
abrupt: sudden and curt, without the smoothness of gradual speech
candid: open, frank, and honest in speaking one's mind
dissuaded: talked out of a plan or course of action by persuasion
doubter: a person who questions or refuses to accept what is said
remit: to send money to someone, usually as payment
vanity: excessive pride in one's own appearance or achievements
awkward: clumsy or uncomfortable, causing embarrassment in dealings
dropt: let fall or abandoned, an old past form of dropped
ask'd: asked, an older spelling of the past tense of ask
propos'd: proposed, suggested as a plan or idea for consideration
show'd: showed, an old spelling meaning displayed or demonstrated
work'd: worked, labored at a task or trade
advis'd: advised, given counsel or recommended a course
hallow'd: made holy or greatly honored, sacred
errand: a short trip made to carry a message or perform a task
discourse: conversation, or a formal speech on a subject
favour: kindness shown to someone, or approval of a request
approbation: formal approval or warm praise given for merit
contrivance: a clever device or plan devised for a particular purpose
reckoning: a calculation of accounts, or a bill to be settled
hints: slight suggestions or indirect clues about something
demand: a strong need or request for goods or services from buyers
calendar: a system of dividing the year into months, days, and dates
reign: the period during which a monarch rules a country
parish: a local church district with its own clergy and community
clergyman: a minister or priest ordained to serve a church
sermons: religious speeches delivered to a congregation, usually from scripture
quakers: members of a Christian group known for simplicity and silent worship
cudgel: a short thick stick used as a weapon or club
jobber: a person who buys and sells goods as a dealer, a middleman
pamphlet: a small unbound booklet or leaflet printed on cheap paper
almanac: a yearly publication of calendars, weather, and useful information
